## Previously ...

- You have a live site
- It emits events with parameters
- You have a consent banner and a statement of success

Now we look at what has actually arrived.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Export GA4 data in a form Tableau can consume
- State the **grain** of a table before you build anything on it
- Distinguish dimensions from measures, and say why the distinction is not cosmetic
- Interrogate the **provenance** of a dataset you did not collect yourself

# 1. Before the Tool: Provenance

## Where Did This Table Come From?

**Provenance** describes the people, systems and decisions involved in
producing, transforming and sharing a dataset.

. . .

It determines quality, reliability and trustworthiness. It is also the part of
an analysis nobody puts on a slide.

. . .

**Treat every provenance claim as a hypothesis to be verified in the data**, not
as documentation to be trusted. Sometimes the documentation is a marketing
document.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
You wrote the measurement plan for your own site three weeks ago. Can you still
say, without checking, what your `key_event` counts include?
:::

## GIGO

Garbage In, Garbage Out. The oldest principle in analytics and still the one
that costs the most.

. . .

Your advantage in this module is unusual: **you are your own data source.** You
can answer provenance questions about your site that no analyst can answer about
a client's.

. . .

Use it. By Lecture 15 you will be documenting cleaning decisions, and the
students who know their own tagging history will finish that lecture in twenty
minutes.

## When Is Zero Not Zero?

<!-- Speaker notes: this is the single most useful habit to install early. Take
     the crime-map example if they need something outside marketing: a map of
     police reports shows almost nothing on the university campus, because
     campus crime is reported to a different force. The blank area is not
     safety, it is a reporting boundary. -->

Three different things arrive in your export looking identical:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**A true zero**

Nobody converted on Tuesday.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**A missing value**

The tag did not fire on Tuesday.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**A boundary**

Tuesday's visitors declined consent.
:::
::::

. . .

Tableau will happily plot all three as a point at zero.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Which of the three would you be most likely to miss on your own site? What check
would catch it?
:::

# 2. Getting Data Out of GA4

## Three Routes Out {.smaller}

| Route | Live? | Effort | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Report export to CSV | No, a snapshot | Minutes | Thresholding, sampling, aggregated fields only |
| Looker Studio connector | Yes | Low | Not Tableau, and not our tool |
| BigQuery export | Yes, event-level | An afternoon of setup | Effectively none, free tier is ample |

. . .

**Our default is the CSV export**, because it is the one you can repeat weekly
without help. We name BigQuery so you know the ceiling you are working under,
and so you can say the word in an interview.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The CSV route gives you rows GA4 has already aggregated. BigQuery gives you one
row per event. Which questions can only be asked at the second grain?
:::

## Data Thresholding

GA4 withholds rows when the numbers are small enough to identify someone,
particularly when Google Signals is on.

. . .

The rows do not appear with a warning. They simply are not there, and your
totals will not reconcile.

. . .

**On a portfolio site with 40 sessions a week, this is not an edge case.** It is
the normal case. Check the data-quality icon on every report you export.

## The Export You Will Use {.smaller}

Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition, then Share → Download CSV.

Set before exporting:

1. **Date range**: from your site's first tagged day to yesterday. Not "last 28
   days", which will silently change meaning every week you re-export.
2. **Dimensions**: session source / medium, session campaign, device category,
   country, landing page.
3. **Metrics**: sessions, engaged sessions, average engagement time, key events,
   session key event rate.
4. **Rows**: raise the row limit. The default truncates and does not tell you.

. . .

Save every export with the date you pulled it in the filename. You will re-pull,
and you will need to know which is which.

# 3. Grain, Dimensions and Measures

## Say the Grain Out Loud

**The grain is what one row is.** Before any chart, finish this sentence: "one
row in this table is one ______".

. . .

GA4 gives you at least three grains, and mixes them freely in the interface:

- **User level**: one row per person (as far as a cookie can tell)
- **Session level**: one row per visit
- **Event level**: one row per thing that happened

. . .

Nearly every wrong number in a marketing dashboard is a metric from one grain
divided by a metric from another.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
"Conversion rate" is a ratio. Name three different numbers that phrase could
mean on your own site, depending on the grain of the numerator and denominator.
:::

## Dimensions versus Measures {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Dimension**

Slices. Blue in Tableau.

Answers "for which group?"

`sessionSource`, `deviceCategory`, `country`, `landingPage`
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Measure**

Aggregates. Green in Tableau.

Answers "how much?"

`sessions`, `keyEvents`, `engagedSessions`
:::
::::

. . .

Tableau guesses when it connects. It guesses from the data type, so a postcode
becomes a measure and Tableau offers you the average postcode.

## The Fields That Are Already Aggregated {.smaller}

| GA4 field | Tableau's guess | What it actually is |
|---|---|---|
| `sessions` | Measure | A count. Safe to sum |
| `keyEvents` | Measure | A count. Safe to sum |
| `averageSessionDuration` | Measure | **Already a mean.** Never sum, never average |
| `sessionKeyEventRate` | Measure | **Already a ratio.** Never average |
| `deviceCategory` | Dimension | Correct |

. . .

**You cannot average an average.** Averaging the mean session duration of mobile
and desktop gives every device equal weight regardless of how many sessions each
had.

## The Trap, With Numbers {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Device | Sessions | Mean duration |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile | 900 | 30s |
| Desktop | 100 | 300s |
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Averaging the averages**

(30 + 300) / 2 = **165s**

**The true mean**

(900×30 + 100×300) / 1000 = **57s**
:::
::::

. . .

A factor of three, from one plausible-looking drag and drop.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The fix is to export a numerator and a denominator and divide them in Tableau,
never to export the ratio. What does that mean for the export you set up in
part 2?
:::

<!-- Speaker notes: this slide is the whole point of the lecture. If they take
     one thing away, it is "export counts, not rates". Lecture 6 then attacks
     the mean itself. -->

# 4. First Views

## Live Demo {background="#43464B"}

1. Connect to the CSV. Watch Tableau assign blue and green, and fix two of them
2. Sessions over time, week not day, so the shape is visible at portfolio volume
3. Break by channel. Note the long tail
4. Break by device. Add the session count as a label next to every rate
5. Break by landing page, and find a page nobody has ever landed on

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

Connect Tableau to your own export and build:

1. Sessions over time
2. Sessions by device category, **with counts shown beside every rate**
3. Sessions by source / medium
4. State the grain of your table in one sentence, written down
5. One view that surprised you, with a sentence saying why

**25 minutes**

# 5. AI for Getting Data Out

## AI This Block: Chat with context

Where we are on the module's AI spine, set out in Lecture 1 and named properly
in Lecture 10:

> **Chat with context**

## Attach the Export, Not a Description of It

This block's step on the AI spine: **stop describing your data and start
attaching it.**

. . .

A description of your data is your model of your data. Attaching the file
removes your model from the loop, which is the point, because your model is what
you are trying to check.

## A Prompt Worth Reusing

> "Here are the first 20 rows of a GA4 export [attached]. Tell me the grain of
> this table, which columns are dimensions and which are measures, and which
> measures are already averages or rates that I must not aggregate again."

. . .

Then the follow-up that does the real work:

> "Which of the columns you just called measures would give a wrong answer if I
> summed it, and what should I export instead?"

## Where It Will Be Wrong

- It will not know your thresholding. It sees rows, not the rows that were
  withheld
- It will read `sessionKeyEventRate` correctly and `conversion_rate_v2`, which
  you named yourself, however it likes
- It will infer the grain from the columns. If your export mixes grains, it will
  confidently pick one

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Verification here is not reading its answer and nodding. It is checking one
column against the GA4 reference, and one row against your own site. Which row
would you check?
:::

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Attach your export and run the prompt above
2. Check its answer against the GA4 dimension and metric reference
3. Note any column it misclassified, and whether the misclassification would
   have changed a number
4. Ask it what is missing from the export that you would need to compute
   conversion rate correctly

**10 minutes**
